doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Detroit musicians arriving in New York
summary: Later colleagues in Oscar Pettiford's band and the Detroit players who arrived in 1956.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Who else would have been in those jam sessions at that time?

Good question. I don’t know. A lot of guys I wound up playing with later in Oscar Pettiford’s band, the guys like Jimmy Cleveland and Jerome Richardson, and Donald Byrd. Well that was later, when the Detroit — that’s another thing — in 1956 there was this mass immigration from Detroit that took over the town. It wasn’t mass, it was maybe a handful of people but they were all great.

There’s something in the water in Detroit. I’m convinced. Because all these guys had the same thing. I called it, it was their version of Charlie Parker, it was this line, this lyrical line that they all knew how to play, like Pepper Adams, Tommy Flanagan, Barry Harris, Billy Mitchell, who wasn’t really from Detroit but he wound up there, Paul Chambers, Kenny Burrell, I’m probably leaving out some. Roland was a little bit different, Roland Hanna. Because he was basically classical pianist that switched to jazz on the influence of Tommy, just a great pianist. And they were amazing. So I played with Tony, I made my first — I made my first record with him.
